tldr: Using monocular depth foundation models off the shelf causes mobile robots to frequently collide due to systematic over-estimation of distances to nearby obstacles. By predicting an uncertainty-aware safe lower bound with a lightweight head of just 0.58M parameters, this method slashes collision rates from 63% to 3% without altering the existing Nav2 stack.
hero_caption: Overall pipeline of the proposed "safe depth" approach. A lightweight head predicts a correction $\mu$ and uncertainty $\sigma$ from frozen Depth Anything V2 features and the RGB image. Using a safety factor $k$ calibrated via conformal prediction, the lower bound $\hat{d}_{\text{safe}}$ is computed and passed to the standard Nav2 stack through an uncertainty-aware ground filter.
overview:
While LiDAR and RGB-D sensors provide robots with accurate distance measurements, their cost, weight, and power consumption remain heavy burdens for small or low-cost platforms. Naturally, recent foundation models for monocular depth estimation, such as Depth Anything V2, offer an attractive alternative using just a single RGB camera. However, plugging these models directly into an existing navigation stack leads to an alarming number of collisions. The models systematically over-estimate distances in unfamiliar scenes, along texture-less walls, and for nearby obstacles.

This paper proposes a lightweight plug-in module that turns predicted depth into "safe depth" without modifying any part of the existing navigation stack (such as Nav2's costmaps or planners). Keeping the pre-trained depth model frozen, it attaches a tiny 0.58M-parameter U-Net head to estimate a per-pixel log-depth correction $\mu$ and uncertainty $\sigma$. The navigation stack then consumes a safe lower bound $\hat{d}_{\text{safe}} = d\,e^{\mu - k\sigma}$, where $k$ is calibrated via split-conformal prediction to provide statistical coverage guarantees. In addition, the paper solves the "phantom floor" problem—where underestimating depth makes a downward-tilted camera perceive the floor as an obstacle—using an uncertainty-aware geometric ground test.

In a simulated indoor benchmark of 120 paired episodes featuring glass, texture-less walls, and dark regions, the proposed approach reduced collision rates from 63% (off-the-shelf) to just 3% (close to the 2% achieved with ground-truth depth), while raising navigation success from 37% to 70%. In contrast, simply applying a uniform safety margin froze the robot by blocking traversable corridors, demonstrating the power of allocating safety margins strictly where uncertainty is high.
contributions: Building a lightweight 0.58M-parameter plug-in head on top of a frozen monocular depth foundation model to predict per-pixel bias correction $\mu$ and uncertainty $\sigma$, providing a safe depth lower bound for standard Nav2.
Identifying the geometric failure mode where computing depth lower bounds with a downward-tilted camera lifts the floor into an obstacle, and resolving it with an uncertainty-aware ground test.

Conducting a rigorous 120-episode paired evaluation with McNemar's test across procedurally generated indoor environments with glass, plain walls, and dark zones, demonstrating the decisive advantage of uncertainty-aware safety over uniform margins.

sections.heading: Why is using monocular depth foundation models directly on robots dangerous?
sections.summary: Advances in monocular depth foundation models promise single-camera navigation, but off-the-shelf models systematically over-estimate distances on unfamiliar areas and texture-less walls. This paper proposes a lightweight plug-in that turns model outputs into safe lower bounds using uncertainty, without touching the navigation stack.
sections.details:
LiDAR and RGB-D cameras are standard sensors for mobile robot obstacle avoidance, but single-camera navigation has long been sought after due to cost, weight, and power constraints on small drones and budget platforms. Recently, depth foundation models such as Depth Anything V2 and Metric3D v2 have demonstrated impressive zero-shot metric depth estimation in unseen environments, prompting attempts to integrate them directly into navigation systems.

However, there is a critical catch: the accuracy of these foundation models is non-uniform. They exhibit large errors on texture-less walls, transparent glass, dark scenes, and out-of-distribution environments. In robotics, the most dangerous failure mode is over-estimating obstacle distances—thinking an object is farther away than it actually is. Under-estimating distance simply makes the robot more cautious, but over-estimating it causes the robot to drive straight into an obstacle. Passing such point clouds directly into a standard Nav2 stack treats all pixels as equally trustworthy, leading to frequent collisions.

This study addresses the problem by introducing uncertainty quantification. Rather than redesigning the planner, it adopts a highly practical approach: a lightweight head sits on top of the frozen model to estimate per-pixel corrections and uncertainties, outputting a statistically calibrated one-sided safe lower bound directly into the Nav2 pipeline.

sections.heading: The evolution of monocular depth, navigation, and uncertainty modeling
sections.summary: Monocular depth estimation has evolved from relative depth to metric foundation models, while navigation research has integrated them with MPC or diffusion models. This study takes a distinct approach: it leaves the classic navigation stack untouched and focuses entirely on making the depth values themselves safe.
sections.details:
Related work spans three main areas:

### Advances in Monocular Depth Estimation
Monocular depth estimation has advanced from early multi-scale CNNs to MiDaS, which enabled zero-shot transfer via multi-dataset mixed training, and further to Depth Anything V2, which distills synthetic data and pseudo-labeled real images. Models like Metric3D v2 normalize camera space to recover real-world scale, providing metric depth across diverse indoor and outdoor environments.

### Monocular Robot Navigation
Attempts to navigate using monocular depth include MonoNav, which uses motion primitives; MonoMPC, which learns collision probabilities from point clouds for risk-aware model predictive control; and NoMaD, which uses diffusion models. However, these methods require custom planners and controllers. This paper takes a different path: it preserves the standard ROS 2 Nav2 stack (costmaps and DWB controller) widely used in industry and academia, making the incoming depth data safe and reliable instead.

### Uncertainty Estimation in Depth
In neural network uncertainty estimation, common approaches include Gaussian negative log-likelihood (NLL) loss to predict variance alongside depth, and post-hoc heads like BayesCap attached to frozen models. Building upon these ideas, this work leverages the statistical framework of conformal prediction to compute a safety factor $k$ with distribution-free pixel coverage guarantees.

sections.heading: How the plug-in architecture turns predicted depth into safe depth
sections.summary: A tiny 0.58M-parameter U-Net head extracts features from frozen Depth Anything V2 to predict log-depth correction $\mu$ and uncertainty $\sigma$. Combined with a conformally calibrated lower bound, it incorporates an uncertainty-aware ground test to prevent downward-tilted camera depth bounds from lifting the floor.
sections.details:
The proposed pipeline consists of a frozen foundation model, a lightweight correction and uncertainty head, conformal calibration for the safe lower bound, and an uncertainty-aware ground test.

### Correction and Uncertainty Prediction Head
The backbone is Depth Anything V2 (ViT-S, pre-trained on Hypersim), kept entirely frozen. The 32-channel feature map immediately preceding the final convolution of the DPT decoder is extracted and concatenated with log-depth $\log d_{\text{DA}}$ and the normalized 3-channel RGB image. These 36 channels are fed into a lightweight U-Net head at half resolution. The head uses dilated convolutions (maximum dilation of 8) and contains only 0.58M parameters. Its output layer is initialized with $\mu = 0$ and $\sigma = 0.2$, ensuring its initial predictions match the base model.

Corrected depth $\hat{d}$ and uncertainty $\sigma$ are parameterized in log-space as $\log \hat{d} = \log d_{\text{DA}} + \mu$ and $s = \log \sigma$. Log-space is chosen because monocular depth errors scale multiplicatively with distance.

### Loss Function Formulation ($\beta$-NLL)
Letting the residual against ground truth be $r = \log d_{\text{GT}} - \log \hat{d}$, standard Gaussian negative log-likelihood is $\mathcal{L}_{\text{NLL}} = \frac{1}{2} r^2 e^{-2s} + s$. However, standard NLL tends to inflate $\sigma$ on difficult pixels rather than correcting $\mu$. To prevent this, the method adopts Seitzer et al.'s $\beta$-NLL, weighting the loss with a stop-gradient term $\text{sg}(\sigma^{2\beta})$ (with $\beta = 0.5$) for stable training. Additionally, a distance-dependent pixel weight $w = 1 / \max(d_{\text{GT}}, 0.5\text{ m})$ emphasizes nearby obstacles that pose direct collision risks.

### Safe Depth Computation and Conformal Calibration
The safe depth passed to the navigation stack is the one-sided lower bound $\hat{d}_{\text{safe}} = d_{\text{DA}} e^{\mu - k\sigma}$. Instead of hand-tuning the safety factor $k$, it is determined via split-conformal calibration on a held-out validation world. Computing the 97.7th percentile of the normalized score $z = (\log \hat{d} - \log d_{\text{GT}}) / \sigma$ on pixels within 3 m yields $k = 3.0$. For a fair baseline, a constant safety margin ($d_{\text{DA}} e^{-c}$) calibrated to the exact same 97.7% coverage yields $c = 0.73$ (scaling distances down by a factor of 0.48).

### Downward-Tilted Cameras and the "Phantom Floor"
This insight is crucial for practical deployment: the robot camera sits 0.55 m above the floor, tilted downward by 0.2 rad. Shrinking depth along viewing rays pulls floor points closer to the camera and simultaneously lifts them upward. A mere 14% depth under-estimation is enough to raise the floor above the voxel costmap obstacle threshold, causing the robot to mistake the entire floor for an impassable obstacle and freeze.

To prevent this, the system calculates the geometric floor distance $d_{\text{floor}}$ from camera pose and intrinsics. If the predicted depth is within a ratio threshold of $d_{\text{floor}}$, it is treated as ground. The proposed method dynamically sets this threshold to $\tau = \max(0.15, k\sigma)$. If the floor plane falls within the pixel's uncertainty band, it is classified as floor and used only to clear costmap voxels rather than marking obstacles.

Passing through an uncertainty-aware ground test, safe depth allows standard Nav2 (green) to operate safely without modification.

sections.heading: Challenging indoor simulation environments and paired evaluations
sections.summary: Using ROS 2 Humble and Gazebo, indoor environments containing glass walls, plain walls, and dark areas were procedurally generated. Across four unseen test environments, 120 paired episodes with slight initial pose perturbations enabled rigorous statistical comparisons between methods.
sections.details:
Simulated experiments were carried out in Gazebo Fortress with ROS 2 Humble.

### Robot and Sensor Configuration
The platform is a differential-drive robot measuring $0.40 \times 0.30\text{ m}$ with a top speed of $0.3\text{ m/s}$. An RGB-D camera ($640 \times 480$ resolution, $60^\circ$ horizontal FOV) is mounted 0.55 m above the floor with a 0.2 rad downward tilt (about $11.5^\circ$). To isolate perception performance from localization drift, ground-truth simulator odometry is used. The Nav2 stack configuration (NavFn planner, DWB controller, voxel costmap, 0.55 m inflation radius) is identical across all evaluated methods.

### Procedural Environment Generation
Environments consist of an 8 m corridor connected to a $7 \times 8\text{ m}$ main room. Three specific challenges can be procedurally inserted: (1) free-standing semi-transparent glass partitions, (2) texture-less white walls, and (3) dark zones with illumination reduced by about 90%. Five worlds were generated for training (one held out for validation and calibration), and four completely separate worlds were used for testing (one plain world and three featuring all three challenges).

### Episode Design and Evaluation Metrics
In each test world, 4 fixed goals and 11 sampled start-goal pairs were tested across 2 runs with small pose perturbations ($\pm 0.1\text{ m}$, $\pm 10^\circ$), totaling 120 paired episodes executed by all methods. Episodes were categorized by difficulty: Easy (clear line of sight), Hard (crossing hazards or narrow passages), and Medium (in between). Metrics include success rate (with 95% Wilson confidence intervals), collision rate, freeze/timeout rate, SPL (Success weighted by Path Length), time to goal, and minimum clearance to obstacles. Differences between methods were tested for statistical significance using McNemar's test.

captions.P4: Test environment (test_01) showing episode start poses (arrows), goals (stars), and A* reference paths color-coded by difficulty (green: Easy, orange: Medium, red: Hard). Cyan bars indicate glass partitions, and magenta panels represent texture-less walls.

sections.heading: From 63% collisions down to 3%: The crucial difference with uniform safety margins
sections.summary: Raw monocular depth collided in 63% of episodes, but safe depth reduced collisions to 3%, closely approaching ground truth (2%). While a uniform safety margin with matching pixel coverage stalled and achieved only 30% success, safe depth achieved a 70% success rate.
sections.details:
Simulation results clearly demonstrate the vital role of uncertainty quantification.

### Dramatic Improvements in Depth Accuracy
Evaluating depth accuracy on the test set (Table I), raw Depth Anything V2 exhibited an average relative error (AbsRel) of 0.262, over-estimating true distance by more than 0.2 m on 59.8% of pixels within 3 m. Adding the proposed head's bias correction ($\mu$) halved AbsRel to 0.134 and reduced near-range over-estimation to 12.0%. The head also demonstrated strong error-ranking capability, achieving a sparsification error AUC of 0.028 on the validation world.

### Closed-Loop Navigation Benchmark
The closed-loop navigation results over 120 episodes (Table II) were:
- **Ground-Truth Depth (GT)**: 93% success, 2% collisions, 0.49 m clearance
- **Raw Depth (Raw)**: 37% success, 63% collisions, 0% freezes, 0.25 m clearance
- **Constant Margin (Margin)**: 30% success, 5% collisions, 65% freezes/timeouts, 0.45 m clearance
- **Bias Correction Only ($\mu$)**: 60% success, 15% collisions, 25% freezes, 0.38 m clearance
- **Safe Depth (Proposed: $\mu - k\sigma$)**: 70% success, 3% collisions, 27% freezes, 0.45 m clearance

Raw monocular depth had 0% freezes or timeouts yet collided in 63% of episodes—a classic symptom of over-confident perception barreling into obstacles. Conversely, the constant margin method reduced collisions to 5% but perceived corridors and gaps between furniture as blocked obstacles, freezing in 65% of episodes. By applying margins selectively only where uncertainty is high, the proposed method kept collisions to 3% while achieving a 70% success rate. In McNemar's test (Table III), safe depth won 52 out of 56 discordant paired episodes against the constant margin ($p = 1 \times 10^{-11}$).

### Breakdown by Hazard Category
Across all hazard categories—glass, plain walls, and dark zones (Table IV)—the performance ranking remained consistent: Raw < $\mu$ < Safe. Glass was the most difficult challenge as it is transparent even to active depth sensors; nevertheless, safe depth achieved a 37% success rate, whereas raw depth achieved 0%.

sections.heading: Where safety margins are spent makes all the difference
sections.summary: Even though the constant margin and safe depth share the same 97.7% pixel-level safety coverage, their navigation success rates differed by 40 percentage points. The paper candidly discusses geometric side effects, simulation dependence, and frame-rate limits.
sections.details:
### Why Uncertainty Modeling Is Essential
Both the constant margin and the proposed method were calibrated on the validation set so that 97.7% of pixels were on the safe side of ground truth. Despite this identical pixel coverage, navigation success differed by 40 percentage points. The reason lies in *where* that safety margin is spent. A constant margin shrinks distances uniformly—even on crisp, high-confidence walls and furniture—destroying traversable space. In contrast, using $\sigma$ enables the robot to move boldly where it is confident and take wide berths only in hard-to-see areas. Furthermore, $\sigma$ captures random residual errors that bias correction $\mu$ alone cannot eliminate, driving the collision rate down from 15% to 3%.

### Geometric Side Effects and Challenges
Taking a depth lower bound inherently introduces geometric distortion into the costmap. While the uncertainty-aware ground test resolved phantom floors, corridor side walls still appear to bulge inward. Most of the 27% failure episodes with safe depth were cases where the robot became overly cautious in narrow corridors and froze. Future improvements could involve calibrating directly against navigation task outcomes rather than pixel coverage, or restricting lower-bound adjustments to near-range obstacles.

### Limitations
The authors explicitly note several limitations:
- All evaluations were conducted in simulation (Gazebo); real-world robot validation is pending.
- The setup was tested with a single robot size, camera pose, and ViT-S backbone.
- Ground-truth odometry was used, leaving the compounded effects of localization drift unexamined.
- The ground test assumes a planar floor.
- Inference runs at roughly 1 Hz on a GTX 1650, which is sufficient for 0.3 m/s but would require higher frame rates for faster platforms.

sections.heading: Conclusion and future directions
sections.summary: This work uncovers the severe collision risks of using monocular depth foundation models off the shelf and solves them via a 0.58M-parameter head with conformally calibrated safe bounds. Future directions include real-robot experiments, task-level calibration, and adaptation to novel scenes.
sections.details:
This paper highlights a serious safety hazard: deploying off-the-shelf monocular depth foundation models directly on mobile robots leads to rampant collisions due to near-range distance over-estimation.

To solve this, the authors introduced a lightweight plug-in module that leverages features from a frozen model to learn bias correction $\mu$ and uncertainty $\sigma$, producing a conformally calibrated lower bound $\hat{d}_{\text{safe}}$. Without altering the existing Nav2 pipeline—and by adding an uncertainty-aware ground test to prevent false obstacle registrations—the method slashed collisions from 63% to 3%, achieving safe and practical navigation. The finding that a naive uniform margin completely freezes the robot underscores the necessity of adaptive, uncertainty-aware margin allocation.

Future work includes real-world deployment, calibrating directly against navigation success rather than pixel-level metrics, and incorporating epistemic uncertainty to handle out-of-distribution environments.

takeaways: Using monocular depth foundation models off the shelf for autonomous navigation causes collisions in over 60% of runs due to near-range distance over-estimation, making safety interventions essential.
Applying a uniform safety margin shrinks open spaces and freezes the robot; selectively allocating margins where uncertainty is high is crucial for success.
Taking lower bounds on a downward-tilted camera lifts the floor into an apparent obstacle; an uncertainty-aware ground test is indispensable to prevent this geometric failure.
Achieving collision rates on par with ground-truth depth requires no changes to the existing Nav2 stack—only adding a 0.58M-parameter lightweight head to a frozen depth model.
limitations: Validation is currently limited to Gazebo simulation with a single robot geometry and fixed camera pose; real-world generalization remains to be proven.
The ground filter assumes a planar floor based on camera tilt, which could fail on ramps, steps, or uneven terrain.
Inference runs at around 1 Hz on an entry-level GPU (GTX 1650); higher frame rates are needed to support robot speeds beyond 0.3 m/s.
